How has the wealth I earned with so much toil gone so lightly? Now, my efforts wasted and penniless, how shall I show my face to my wife or to my friends?" Having resolved this, he went once more to Vardhamānapura <note>a city, literally "the Flourishing City", where he had earned his first fortune</note>. There, in just a single year, he earned five hundred pieces of gold, and once again set out for home, this time by another road.

Just as the sun was setting, he reached that very same banyan tree. "Alas, alas! What has this wretched Fate set in motion now? Here again is that same demon <note>original: "rākṣasa", an ogre</note> in the shape of a banyan!" As he was thinking this, half as if in a dream, he saw on its branch the very same two men. One of them said: "Doer! Why did you give this Somilaka five hundred pieces of gold? Do you not know that, beyond food and clothing, nothing more at all is his?" The other replied: "Sir Destiny <note>original: "karman", deed or fate; the two figures personify a man's own effort and the destiny fixed by his past deeds</note>, I must give to those who strive. What becomes of it rests with you. So why do you reproach me?" When he heard this, Somilaka searched for his knot of gold and found it empty. Then, overcome by utter despair, he thought: "Alas! What use is life to me, now that I am without wealth? I will hang myself here on this banyan tree and give up my life."

Having resolved this, he made a rope of <term>darbha</term> <gloss>a sacred grass</gloss>, fitted the noose around his neck, climbed onto the branch, tied the rope to it, and was just about to throw himself off, when a man standing in the sky said this: "Ho, Somilaka! <summary>Somilaka, robbed a second time by Destiny of the gold he has toiled to earn, overhears the personified Doer and Destiny arguing about him beneath the same banyan tree. In despair he tries to hang himself, but a voice from the sky, the very power that takes away his wealth, calls on him to stop.</summary>
